people.name: Melba Liston
people.description: American jazz trombonist, musical arranger, and composer (1926–1999)
albums: Live at the Five Spot (Randy Weston album)

interviews.label: Melba Liston
interviews.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.
quotes.summary: Liston said she had written for Weston until her stroke and was writing for him again, that he helped pull her out of it, and thanked him for sticking with her when nobody else did.

quotes.quote: Randy, I have all the freedom I want.
quotes.summary: Liston said that, unlike clients who dictated what they wanted, Weston gave her all the freedom she wanted as his arranger.

quotes.quote: Then I met Randy [Weston] when I was playing with Dizzy, and he said he wanted me to copy or something for him.
quotes.summary: Liston recalled meeting Weston while she was playing with Dizzy Gillespie, when he asked her to copy music for him, which turned into her writing for him.

quotes.quote: Randy pulled me out of the stroke, so I have to go with him.
quotes.summary: Liston said that in planning her return to New York she put Weston first, because he had pulled her out of the stroke.

quotes.quote: Randy likes Thelonious much.
quotes.summary: After Bryant heard a Monk flavour in Little Niles, Liston said Weston was very fond of Thelonious Monk.

quotes.quote: Randy tells me how many choruses he’s going to take and where violins come in, but nothing else.
quotes.summary: Liston said that Weston told her only how many choruses he would take and where the violins came in, leaving everything else to her.

quotes.quote: Yeah, but I think Randy pushed me along.
quotes.summary: Asked about relearning everything after her stroke, Liston said she thought Weston pushed her along.

quotes.quote: Oh yeah, but Randy helped me to get started writing, and so I’m doing it.
quotes.summary: Liston said Weston helped her start writing again after her stroke, though she was not yet writing as fast as before.

he_said.summary: Weston said only Melba Liston could arrange “Spirit of Our Ancestors”, told how he goaded her back to work after her stroke — she learned to write music on a computer with her left hand — and recalled her arrangements arriving from a California hospital in time for the 1959 Five Spot date and the 1985 Montreal concert.
he_said.one_liner: his arranger; wrote left-handed after her stroke
he_said.his_quote: I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know?

people.name: Benny Powell
people.image: Count Basie and His Orchestra performs in Helsinki 1962 (JOKAHBL3E C04-11).tif

interviews.label: Benny Powell
interviews.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

interviews.label: Benny Powell
interviews.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

quotes.quote: He said, “BP,” most people who like me call me BP, he said, “I’m just trying to put the magic back in music.” And boy can he ever do it. He is a spellbinder.
quotes.summary: Powell said that when he joined Weston fifteen years earlier, Weston told him he was 'just trying to put the magic back in music', called him a spellbinder who leads by example like Count Basie, and said Weston gave him room to create his own parts.

quotes.quote: I work with him now, and it’s a real joy to work with him. Every time he sits down at the piano, even if it’s just, well usually he does it when we play concerts, he gets antsy, but he never fools around. It sounds like a concerto every time he sits down.
quotes.summary: Powell called Weston the greatest pianist in the world and said it was a joy to work with him, because every time he sat down at the piano it sounded like a concerto.

quotes.quote: One of those mornings he knocked on my door at seven o’clock and said, “Benny, can I help you with your bags out?” I said, “Man, you’re the boss, I’m supposed to be helping you,” I said, “You don’t know how to be a boss man, you’re supposed to be tough.” But he’s just a wonderful — I can’t sing his praises enough.
quotes.summary: Powell told how Weston arranged dialysis for him three times a week on European tours, had the back of the tour bus made into a bed for him, and offered to carry the trombonist's bags, which made Powell call him an example of an employer who understands an employee's problems.

quotes.quote: I’ve been playing with Randy Weston for about the last 15 years, and it’s really been glorious what I’ve been through.
quotes.summary: Powell recalled going to Morocco with Weston about seven years earlier to film his return there, said fifteen years in his band had been glorious, and told how Weston's father had told him he was an African born in America.

quotes.quote: Oh he is. Exceptionally spiritual. He is the most scholarly person I know.
quotes.summary: Powell agreed that Weston was exceptionally spiritual, called him the most scholarly person he knew, and said Weston and his bandmates spent their days off researching in libraries.

quotes.quote: For example we were coming back from Jamaica and I saw him, as always, he is always the smoothest guy at the airport, because no matter what language it is, he has such a nice demeanor, and I don’t know what he’s saying but it sounds like he’s saying I’m a nice guy, give me a break, and you’re a nice person.
quotes.summary: Powell called Weston's communication skills magnificent and told how, flying back from Jamaica, Weston charmed a ticket agent into putting a load of percussion on his first-class ticket while telling the band how pretty she was.

quotes.quote: way, he’s like Duke Ellington. He can meld anything because I think, well I don’t know, he has just the most beautiful organizational sense.
quotes.summary: Powell compared Weston to Duke Ellington, saying he could meld anything thanks to his beautiful organizational sense, so that within minutes of starting with Moroccan musicians the band sounded as if they had worked together for years.

quotes.quote: She’s been wheelchair bound for a little while, but she and Randy are very close, and he really looks out — oh he’s a wonderful human being.
quotes.summary: Powell said Melba Liston and Weston were very close, that Weston looked out for her, and called him a wonderful human being, which leads into his dialysis story.

he_said.summary: Weston named Powell in his band on “Saga”, “Khepera”, Montreal, the Brooklyn church concert and St. Lucia, and recalled him crying “We have adventure!” as the sextet rode donkeys up to Jajouka — echoing the line Jenkins quoted from Powell, his trombonist of many years.
he_said.one_liner: trombonist; cried “we have adventure!” on the donkeys
he_said.his_quote: Benny said, “We have adventure! We have adventure!”

interviews.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

interviews.label: Orrin Keepnews
interviews.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: We had some recent albums on the wall, including a couple of Randy Weston. I had, no, I look around and saw that Miles was looking at these things and I was…and he said, “Oh, Randy! I’m glad somebody got around to recording him. It should have been done along time ago,” and I said, “Well if you feel that way about Randy, why didn’t you recommend him to your label?”
quotes.summary: Keepnews recalled Miles Davis seeing Weston's Riverside albums on his office wall and saying he was glad somebody had finally recorded him, then refusing with scorn to recommend anyone to his own label boss, Bob Weinstock.

quotes.quote: But we weren’t a hundred percent sure, and it was another number that got tremendous reaction, this was the first recording as far as I know of Randy Weston’s “High Fly” which of course has become quite a classic in its own right, and so we put that as the first number on the B side, as a back-up.
quotes.summary: Keepnews said Cannonball Adderley's live album held what he believed was the first recording of Weston's 'Hi-Fly', by then a classic, and that Cannonball introduced it by calling Weston the waltz king of jazz.

quotes.quote: before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats.
quotes.summary: Keepnews named Weston among the easygoing artists ('all pussycats') he had recorded before the formidable Thelonious Monk.

interviews.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

quotes.quote: First time I went to Africa was because of Randy Weston.
quotes.summary: Laws said his first trip to Africa came about because of Weston.

quotes.quote: Randy Weston, I think he – I don’t know if he lived there.
quotes.summary: Laws described playing in Tangier with other CTI artists and hearing Moroccan flute players, and was unsure whether Weston lived there.

people.name: Ahmed Abdul-Malik
albums: The Modern Art of Jazz by Randy Weston

he_said.summary: Weston named Abdul-Malik on oud in his 1974 European touring group and among the musicians at the festival he organised in Tangier in 1972.
he_said.one_liner: played oud on his 1974 european tour
he_said.his_quote: I had Ahmed Abdul- Malik on the oud; I had William Allen on bass, myself at the piano, Steve Berrios on percussion cause my son couldn’t make it. We toured, the first time, to play Europe.

he_said.summary: Weston named him as the bassist in his quartet for the “Three African Queens” performance with the Boston Pops.
he_said.one_liner: bass for three african queens, boston pops
he_said.his_quote: With me, I had Idrees Sulieman on trumpet; I had Frank Gap on drums, Jamie Onaso on bass, and myself on piano.

people.name: Sam Gill
albums: Cole Porter in a Modern Mood
Get Happy with the Randy Weston Trio

he_said.summary: Weston said Riverside wanted his first record to be solo piano, he wanted a trio, and they compromised on a duo with Sam Gill on bass for the Cole Porter album.
he_said.one_liner: bass on his first record, cole porter, 1954
he_said.his_quote: Finally, we compromised with myself and Sam Gill on bass. So, my first recording of Cole Porter was piano and bass, but they wanted me to do solo piano.

he_said.summary: Weston named Harper on “Saga”, the jazz night at Montreal in 1997 and the 1972 Tangier festival, and recalled that on the trip to Jajouka he was the only one who stayed cool because, being from Texas, he could ride donkeys.
he_said.one_liner: from texas, could ride donkeys to jajouka
he_said.his_quote: Billy Harper was the only one that was cool, because Billy, being from Texas, he knew how to ride horses and donkeys.

people.name: Dizzy Gillespie
albums: Charles Mingus and Friends in Concert

he_said.summary: Weston named Gillespie among the masters he had 'spiritual contact' with and whose hands he touched, and in the baton-passing image of jazz tradition.
he_said.one_liner: a master whose hand he touched
he_said.his_quote: I had the spiritual contact with Count Basie, or Coleman Hawkins, or Dizzy Gillespie. I saw them, I touched their hands, you see?

he_said.summary: Weston named Sulieman as the trumpeter in his quartet for the “Three African Queens” performance with the Boston Pops.
he_said.one_liner: trumpet for three african queens, boston pops
he_said.his_quote: With me, I had Idrees Sulieman on trumpet; I had Frank Gap on drums, Jamie Onaso on bass, and myself on piano.

he_said.summary: Weston named TK Blue in his bands from the 1985 Montreal ten-piece through the 1997 residency, the Brooklyn church concert and St. Lucia, and recalled him and “the guys” coming to the church to pray for his sister the day before her burial in 2001.
he_said.one_liner: prayed with the band for his sister
he_said.his_quote: Exactly, but the day before TK Blue and the guys came to the church and they all prayed for my sister in the church.

he_said.summary: Weston called Blake one of his “regular guys”, the bassist of his trio on “Zep Tepi”, and named him on “Saga”, “Khepera”, the 1997 Montreal residency, the Brooklyn church concert, St. Lucia, and as the one he took to the Kamigamo Shinto shrine.
he_said.one_liner: regular trio bassist; took him to kyoto
he_said.his_quote: I had my regular guys: Alex Blake and Neil Clark.

he_said.summary: Weston said Olatunji and his traditional group of dancers and musicians opened the Brooklyn church concert with the Gnawa that became 'Spirit: The Power of Music'.
he_said.one_liner: opened his gnawa church concert in brooklyn
he_said.his_quote: It was powerful because at that particular concert we opened up with Babatunde Olatunji, with his traditional group of dancers and music.
he_said.instrument_or_role: leader of a traditional group of dancers and music

he_said.summary: Weston named “the great Benny Bailey” first in his ten-piece group at the 1985 Montreal Jazz Festival, for which Melba Liston’s music arrived from her hospital bed.
he_said.one_liner: in his 1985 montreal ten-piece
he_said.his_quote: I had a ten-piece group of the great Benny Bailey, Sahib Shihab, TK Blue, Clyde Lucas on drums, Mohammad Bin Fata, the Gnawa playing African percussion, myself on piano, Woodward Little was on bass.

people.name: Coleman Hawkins
albums: Live at the Five Spot (Randy Weston album)

he_said.summary: Weston called Coleman Hawkins his idol — at 17 he bought three copies of “Body and Soul” and hid two — and said recording with him live at the Five Spot in 1959 was another miracle.
he_said.one_liner: his idol; on his 1959 five spot date
he_said.his_quote: A good example of that is this, when we did the date with Coleman Hawkins, which was another miracle for me because Coleman Hawkins was my idol. When “Body and Soul” came out I was 17 years old. I bought 3 copies and I hid two.

he_said.one_liner: president of verve; made ten cds with him
he_said.his_quote: Philippe Alad, and he is the one that I did ten C.D.s with, so I was very happy about that date.

he_said.summary: Weston said that normally Johnny Copeland sang the blues with them, but he could not make the 1997 Montreal blues night.
he_said.one_liner: normally sang the blues with them
he_said.his_quote: It came out on an album called “Volcano”, and normally we would have a guy, Johnny Copeland, singing the blues but Johnny couldn’t make it.

people.name: Max Roach
people.description: American jazz percussionist, drummer, and composer (1924–2007)

he_said.summary: Weston said he brought Max Roach's band, without Max himself, to his 1972 festival in Tangiers.
he_said.one_liner: his band came to tangiers without him
he_said.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.

he_said.summary: Weston counted Clarke among his “regular guys” in the “Zep Tepi” trio and named him in his bands on “Saga”, at Montreal in 1997, at the Brooklyn church concert and in St. Lucia.
he_said.one_liner: a regular guy, from saga to zep tepi
he_said.his_quote: I had my regular guys: Alex Blake and Neil Clark.

he_said.summary: Weston said 'the great' Pharoah Sanders was on the 'Khepera' date, where they recorded the Gnawa piece 'Blue Moses' together.
he_said.one_liner: played blue moses with him on khepera
he_said.his_quote: On that date, we also had the great Pharaoh Sanders. With Pharaoh Sanders we did one of the Gnawa pieces, “Blue Moses”
